name: The Holm Oak of the Lampedusa Sanctuary, Castellaro

location.address: Santuario di Nostra Signora di Lampedusa, Castellaro

story:
The sanctuary this holm oak stands beside was founded on an escape story. In 1561, the legend goes, a man from Castellaro named Andrea Anfosso was captured by Turkish raiders and taken to the island of Lampedusa, broke free, built a makeshift boat and sailed home using a painting of the Madonna as his sail. That image is still venerated inside.

The path up to the sanctuary climbs through old holm oaks, and Italy's national list of monumental trees picks out this one at the sanctuary itself: 3.65 metres round and 13 metres tall. The writer Giovanni Ruffini set a scene of his nineteenth-century novel Il Dottor Antonio here, so you can compare his descriptions with the hill as it is now.

The holm oak is the evergreen oak of the Mediterranean, with dark, leathery leaves that are grey and felted underneath, and in a dry place like this hilltop it grows slowly. Nobody has published how old this one is. If you know, tell us.

Our pin is the register's point. It stands at a place of pilgrimage open to all, and seeing it costs nothing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad evergreen crown of dark, leathery leaves and a thick trunk more than three and a half metres round, beside the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lampedusa on the hilltop above Castellaro.
access: Free: at the sanctuary, reached by road or by the footpath up from Castellaro.
transport: In the hills between Taggia and Sanremo, about 13 km straight line from Pontedassio; by car is easiest.

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), no. 01/C143/IM/07

verify_notes: MASAF register 01/C143/IM/07: Quercus ilex, Castellaro, Chiesa Nostra Signora di Lampedusa, girth 365 cm, height 13 m, 43.873767, 7.863958. Riviera dei Fiori DMO page on Castellaro: centuries-old holm oaks lead to the hilltop sanctuary; Anfosso legend of 1561; Ruffini's Il Dottor Antonio sets a scene at the sanctuary (the page says Andrea Ruffini; the novel's author is Giovanni Ruffini, en.wikipedia Doctor Antonio). name: The Horse Chestnut of San Bernardino, Triora
story:
The church of San Bernardino is dedicated to Saint Bernardino of Siena, who came to preach in Triora around 1418, and its walls carry fifteenth-century frescoes, among them a Last Judgement crowded with demons, women in mitres and heretics in the flames. Outside it, Italy's national list of monumental trees records a horse chestnut 3.1 metres round and 20 metres tall.

It is the smaller of Triora's three listed horse chestnuts; the other two stand together by the church of Sant'Agostino, a few hundred metres away, so all three make one short walk. The witch trials that began here in 1588 are told in the village's Museum of Ethnology and Witchcraft.

The horse chestnut is a mountain tree from the Balkans, planted across Europe for its shade. In May it carries upright candles of white flowers flecked with pink and yellow, and in autumn it drops shiny brown conkers from spiky cases, while its big hand-shaped leaves turn yellow and rust.

Nobody has published how old it is. If you know, tell us. It stands by a church and costs nothing to see.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big horse chestnut beside the church of San Bernardino in Triora, with large hand-shaped leaves of five to seven leaflets.
access: Free: beside the church of San Bernardino.
transport: In Triora, about 360 m from the Sant'Agostino horse chestnuts.

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), no. 04/L430/IM/07

verify_notes: MASAF register 04/L430/IM/07: Aesculus hippocastanum, Triora, Chiesa di San Bernardino, girth 310 cm, height 20 m, 43.991728, 7.763914. ligurialetters.substack.com (2023, read in full): San Bernardino dedicated to Bernardino of Siena, who came to Triora around 1418; fifteenth-century frescoes including Il Giudizio Universale with demonic creatures, women wearing mitres and heretics being burned; Museo etnografico e della Stregoneria; accusations in 1588.
